title: handshake-retry-mode-repro-trace
content:
TL;DR: intermittent TLS client_hello retransmits from private-deploy hosts when peered to customer VPCs. Symptoms cluster during bursts and seem correlated with PMTU/pmtud fragments and a mid-path device rewriting SYN options. Repro steps below + packet extracts and commands we ran. Hypothesis: a network middlebox between the private egress NAT and peered subnet drops large TLS client_hello or causes path MTU blackhole, leading to client retransmit/backoff and the serving runtime closing the k-v cache early. Immediate workaround: reduce initial client_hello size (no SNI list, disable ALPN extras) and set kernel tcp_retries2/tcp_retries1 higher for bursts. Not ideal.

Observed behavior:
- Affected hosts: private-deploy nodes in us-west-2 within customer VPC peering paths (subset of customers, not all).
- Symptom: outbound connections to model-hosted endpoints occasionally show TLS handshake stalls; client retransmits client_hello (packet seen twice) then server responds once, client times out and fallback code path triggers a cold start model variant (higher latency) or a fallback model.
- Failure rate: ~2.4% of handshakes during bursty traffic window (09:00-09:30 UTC), spike to 8% during small window.
- Errors seen in runtime logs: "TLS handshake failed: timeout waiting for server response" and downstream: "kv-cache miss due to connection reset".

What we ran (commands + notable outputs):
- tcpdump on node capturing SYN/ACK/ClientHello
  sudo tcpdump -s 0 -w /tmp/trace1.pcap host 10.2.7.104 and port 443
  Observed: client_hello frame length 1586 bytes, seen, then retransmit at t+250ms, server never responded to first, responded to retransmit.

- tshark extract of client_hello lengths:
  tshark -r /tmp/trace1.pcap -Y "tls.handshake.type == 1" -T fields -e frame.time_relative -e tls.handshake.length
  outputs:
    0.123	1586
    0.375	1586
  Interpretation: identical payload retransmitted, suggests first packet got lost or blackholed.

- tcpdump on peering router (mirror) shows ICMP "Fragmentation needed" for initial packet
  ICMP type 3 code 4, mtu=1400 for that path
  Correlates: client_hello size > 1400 -> needs fragmentation -> PMTU blackhole plausible if ICMP blocked upstream.

- openssl s_client probe from node (repro):
  openssl s_client -connect model-host:443 -msg -debug
  Result: handshake completes if we force MTU smaller (for example setting IP_MTU? not trivial). When using curl with --ciphers or disabling some extensions handshake shrinks and succeeds consistently.

- iptables/nftables checks:
  No explicit MSS clamp on node. No iptables raw rules dropping ICMP.

- sysctl values checked:
  sysctl net.ipv4.ip_no_pmtu_disc = 0 (we honor PMTU)
  sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing = 0 (no probing enabled)

Reproduction steps (how to reproduce quickly):
1) From private node: run a short script that opens many concurrent TLS connections with a large ClientHello (ALPN+SNI+OCSP stapling request) to target host.
2) Observe ~1-3% of connections retransmit client_hello once then either succeed later or timeout depending on whether ICMP fragmentation messages traverse path.

Quick repro script (bash):
- python3 repro_open_tls.py (attached locally)
- simplified curl loop:
  for i in {1..1000}; do curl -sS --http2 -H "Host: model-host" https://model-host:443 >/dev/null & done

Packet snippets (abbreviated):
- frame 1023: 10.2.7.104 -> 54.245.33.101 TCP 443
  Flags [P.], seq 335..1921, len 1586
  TLSv1.3 Client Hello (len=1586)
- frame 1027: ICMP 54.245.33.1 -> 10.2.7.104 Type 3 Code 4 (Fragmentation needed) Next-Hop MTU 1400
- frame 1031: retransmit from 10.2.7.104 seq 335..1921 len 1586
- frame 1035: server -> client TCP ACK; TLS handshake proceeds

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) PMTU blackhole on specific peering paths due to upstream ACL blocking ICMP type 3 code 4. Initial packet is dropped by middlebox (inspects >1400 and drops) and ICMP not returned to client, causing retransmission. When retransmit happens later fragmentation/ip stack chooses path differently or router responds. Result: increased latency and occasional failure windows.
2) Middlebox rewriting SYN options (MSS) strips/changes MSS causing mismatch and large first packet dropped; subsequent retransmit uses smaller MSS or path changes.
3) SNI/ALPN extension length pushes client_hello > baseline; servers with SYN cookies or rate-limiters may drop first handshake in bursts.
4) Asymmetric routing: ICMP replies go back a different path and don't reach origin because of source-NATing on egress, causing PMTU signals to be lost.

Evidence mapping to hypotheses:
- ICMP frag-needed observed -> supports PMTU blackhole (#1).
- No MSS clamp on node, but peering router config unknown -> possible #2.
- Reproduced by shrinking TLS ext list and then handshake success -> supports SNI+ALPN size being a trigger (#3).
- Packet mirror shows ICMP returning from mid-path, but node not receiving it until later -> could be asymmetry (#4).

Immediate mitigations tried (and outcomes):
- Set net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1 (probe) on sample nodes -> reduced failures to ~0.2% in short run. Not production-wide yet.
- Quick app-level change: remove extra ALPN entries and reduced SNI list -> dropped client_hello size from 1586 to 900 and resolved intermittent failures for customers in test group.
- Applied iptables MSS clamp on some nodes (mss 1400) -> immediate improvement but might hide underlying peering issue; need infra approval for blanket clamp.

Next steps (owners and tickets):
- Infra network: capture mirrored pcap on peering router for impacted customer peerings (owner: Jordan Lee) - linear PRIV-328
- Engage customer network ops to verify ICMP filtering on their edge (owner: Mateo) - include pcap and timestamps
- Experiment with enabling tcp_mtu_probing=2 for a week on staging fleet (owner: Samira)
- Add probing-based fallback in runtime to retry handshake with reduced extensions when first handshake fails (engineering task: runtime/handshake-fallback PR 877)
- Long term: if customers cannot enable ICMP allow, consider infrastructure-level MSS clamping at egress devices (proposal required)

Questions I still have / TODO:
- Does peering router perform any TCP normalization? (SYN rewriting, MSS change) - need config review.
- Which customers' edge devices are more likely to drop large TLS client_hello? Correlate with customer edge vendor (F5, Palo Alto, Fortinet).
- Should we enable tcp_mtu_probing by default on all private-deploy nodes? Risk: transient overhead.

Notes for oncall handoff:
- Primary symptom: TLS stalls during bursts -> check tcpdump for tls.client_hello length > 1400 and look for ICMP type3 code4 arriving shortly after.
- Temp mitigations: enable tcp_mtu_probing=1 and reduce ALPN/SNI sizes, apply per-node MSS clamp if necessary.
- Logs to collect: /var/log/runtime/*.log around timestamp, /tmp/trace*.pcap, ip route get <target>, sysctl values.

Related artifacts and quick refs:
- quick tshark one-liner to find frag-needed: tshark -r /tmp/trace.pcap -Y "icmp.type == 3 && icmp.code == 4" -T fields -e frame.number -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e icmp.frag_needed.mtu
- curl flag to reduce TLS extensions: curl --http1.1 --no-alpn --tlsv1.2 -H "Host: model-host" https://model-host:443

Open: whether this is a transient misconfiguration on customer side or systemic change in interconnects. For now, add a short-run runtime mitigation (handshake fallback) and continue network-level investigation.

Scratchpad / raw commands tried during session (for reproducibility):
- sudo tcpdump -s0 -i eth0 host 54.245.33.101 and port 443 -w /tmp/trace.pcap
- sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0 "icmp and src host 54.245.33.1" -vv
- tshark -r /tmp/trace.pcap -Y "tls.handshake.type == 1" -T fields -e frame.number -e frame.time_relative -e tls.handshake.length
- sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1
- curl --http1.1 --no-alpn -v https://model-host:443
- openssl s_client -connect model-host:443 -servername model-host -tls1_3 -msg -debug
- sudo iptables -t mangle -A POSTROUTING -p tcp --dport 443 -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu

If replicating, keep a copy of the raw pcap and attach in the ticket (pcap pinned: /tmp/priv-peering-march05.pcap).
